1. Welcome — how to read this book

This book walks you through the whole DokTool code base, from the first line the server runs to the last button of the mobile app. Its goal is simple: after reading it, you should be able to open any file and say what it does, why it is there and what happens when someone presses a button — as if you had written it yourself.

1.1 How the book is organised

  • Part 1 — Foundations (chapters 1–3). What DokTool is, how the repository is laid out, and how the three applications talk to each other.
  • Part 2 — The API (chapters 4–8). The NestJS server: how a request is handled, then every module — accounts, access, content, calculators, pregnancy, verification, payments, finance, analytics and the admin side.
  • Part 3 — Admin Web (chapters 9–10). The Next.js console the team uses: its building blocks, then every screen and button.
  • Part 4 — The mobile app (chapters 11–12). The Flutter app: its foundations, then every screen and button.
  • Part 5 — Journeys (chapter 13). Eight complete stories followed through all three applications, step by step.
  • Part 6 — Working on the code (chapter 14). Tests, CI, and recipes for the changes you will make most often.
  • Appendix A. Generated from the code: every file, every documented function and every commented button, in the order of the file. It is the reference you keep open next to the editor.
How to study. Read a chapter, then open the files it names in your editor and read them top to bottom. Every function and every button now has a short comment explaining it (that was part of the October 2026 audit). Code shown in this book is not retyped: it is pulled from the files when the book is built, with its real line numbers, so what you read here is exactly what is in the repository.

1.2 What DokTool is

DokTool is a mobile clinical utility for doctors, residents and medical students in Algeria. It is deliberately small and fast. It is not a patient record, a prescription generator, a drug database, a chatbot or a marketing platform. It offers four things:

ResourceWhat the doctor does with it
Ordonnances (prescription models)Searches, finds a reference model and reads it as a PDF. Read-only: no editing, no patient field, no printing, no sharing.
Certificats (certificate models)The same, for medical certificates.
Calculateurs (clinical calculators)Picks a score or formula, enters validated values, gets a result with its interpretation band and its published source.
Grossesse · Allaitement (pregnancy and lactation)Looks up a substance and reads, per trimester and for breastfeeding, the conduct and the evidence level — always separate, never a "safe / unsafe" verdict.

The product summary in CLAUDE.md fits in three lines, and the whole code base serves them:

References SEARCH → FIND REFERENCE MODEL → VIEW PDF → USE AS CLINICAL REFERENCE Calculators SELECT TOOL → ENTER VALIDATED INPUTS → CALCULATE → REVIEW RESULT + SOURCE → DONE Prospects DEMO → EXPLORE → UNDERSTAND → SUBSCRIBE

1.3 Who uses it

PersonApplicationWhat they can do
Doctor or resident, verified and subscribed (« Pro »)MobileEverything: every model, calculator and profile, offline copies.
Doctor or resident not yet subscribedMobileA real account with the demo sample set. May buy once their professional status is verified.
Medical student, verifiedMobileFree: the calculators; models and profiles are visible as titles only (locked), except the demo samples. No purchase.
Demo visitorMobileNo sign-up, no contact data, no time limit: the demo sample items only. The demo is an access context, not a kind of person.
Admins (Super Admin, editors, reviewers, finance…)Admin WebUpload models, author and review calculators and profiles, verify professionals, manage plans, read finance, analytics and the audit log — each according to their grants.

1.4 The rules every line of code respects

These rules come from the Product Owner's decisions (docs/adr/ADR-006-product-owner-decisions.md) and the design system. Whenever you wonder "why is this code so careful here?", the answer is usually one of them.

1. The backend decides access. The server computes an AccessProfile (tier + the state of every feature) and re-checks it on every endpoint. The app only draws what it receives; it never says if (student).
2. Locked is not hidden. A locked item stays visible with its lock and the reason. Only deferred modules (drug database, prescription generation…) are never shown at all.
3. No patient data, anywhere. Calculator inputs never leave the phone; analytics carry no free text, no search words and no input values.
4. Reference PDFs are read-only. No editor, no export, no print, no share, no download button. Files live in private storage and are reached only through short-lived signed URLs.
5. Clinical content is never invented. A calculator formula comes from a cited source, is reviewed by someone other than its author, has test cases, and is immutable once published. AI never writes or changes a formula or a profile.
6. Calm money. Subscriptions show what is included, the price, the duration and « non remboursable », with no red, no countdown and no refund workflow.
7. Bilingual from one catalogue. French and English for every text, from packages/i18n. No Arabic or right-to-left inside the app itself.

1.5 Words you will meet everywhere

Word in the codeMeaning
TierWhere a person lands: DEMO · STUDENT · PROFESSIONAL_UNPAID · PROFESSIONAL · RESTRICTED.
FeatureKeyA capability the policy decides: search, reference.view, calculator.use, offline.sync, subscription.purchase…
LockReason / UnlockPathWhy something is locked (SUBSCRIPTION_REQUIRED, VERIFICATION_PENDING…) and the one screen that can unlock it.
demoSampleA flag on content: this item is part of the free sample set (demo, unpaid professionals, students).
ViewerWhoever is looking at content: a signed-in user or a demo session.
GrantAn admin permission, like calculators.publish or finance.read.
Version (calculator, profile, plan)Clinical content and prices are versioned: a published version never changes; a change is a new version.
DomainErrorThe one way the API refuses something: a stable code the apps translate.

2. The repository — where everything lives

DokTool is one Git repository (a monorepo) holding three applications and four shared packages. The web console and the mobile app are already completely separate: they live in different folders, use different languages and frameworks, and never import each other's code. What they share is a contract with the server, generated automatically.

2.1 The top-level folders

doktool/ ├── apps/ │ ├── api/ ← the server (NestJS, TypeScript). The ONLY part that touches the database. │ │ ├── src/ code: main.ts, app.module.ts, common/, config/, infrastructure/, modules/, scripts/ │ │ ├── prisma/ schema.prisma (47 tables) + migrations/ (hand-written SQL) │ │ └── test/ unit/ (pure logic) and integration/ (real HTTP + real PostgreSQL) │ ├── admin/ ← Admin Web (Next.js, React, TypeScript). The team's browser console. │ │ ├── src/app/ the pages (one folder = one URL) │ │ ├── src/features/ the screens, one folder per console section │ │ ├── src/ui/ the shared components (Button, DataTable, Dialog, Drawer…) │ │ └── src/api/ the typed API client (schema.d.ts is generated) │ └── mobile/ ← the app (Flutter, Dart) for iOS and Android. │ ├── lib/src/core/ networking, session, local database, secure storage │ ├── lib/src/features/ one folder per feature (onboarding, library, calculators…) │ ├── lib/src/ui/ the shared widgets (DtButton, DtAlert, ContentRow…) │ └── test/ widget and unit tests ├── packages/ │ ├── api-contract/ openapi.json — the contract both clients are generated from │ ├── design-tokens/ colours, spacing, radii… → CSS, Tailwind, TypeScript and Dart │ ├── i18n/ messages.fr.json + messages.en.json → Flutter ARB + admin catalogue │ └── calculator-vectors/ test cases both calculator engines must pass ├── design/ the design system: specifications, component cards, tokens.json └── docs/ decisions (adr/), audits, operations guides, this book

2.2 How the web app and the mobile app are separated

The question "where is the web code, where is the mobile code?" has a clean answer:

Admin WebMobile app
Folderapps/adminapps/mobile
LanguageTypeScript + React (TSX)Dart
FrameworkNext.js (App Router)Flutter
Who uses itThe DokTool team, on a computer (≥ 1024 px)Doctors, residents, students, demo visitors, on a phone
API it calls/admin/v1/* with a session cookie + 2FA/v1/* with a bearer token
Generated clientapps/admin/src/api/schema.d.tsapps/mobile/lib/src/core/api/generated/
Package managernpm (workspace)flutter pub
TestsVitest (apps/admin/src/test)flutter test (apps/mobile/test)

The only things they have in common come from packages/: the same words (i18n), the same colours (design tokens) and the same API contract. None of these is imported as source code; each is generated into the format the app needs.

design/system/tokens.json ──generate──► tokens.css + tailwind preset (admin) + doktool_tokens.dart (mobile) packages/i18n/messages.*.json ─build──► admin catalogue (TS) + lib/l10n/*.arb (mobile) apps/api (decorators) ──openapi──► packages/api-contract/openapi.json ──► schema.d.ts (admin) + Dart client (mobile)
Never edit a generated file by hand. schema.d.ts, everything under core/api/generated/, doktool_tokens.dart and the ARB files are rewritten by their generators. CI compares them with a fresh generation and fails on any difference ("drift").

2.3 How the three applications talk

┌────────────────────┐ HTTPS /v1/* (Bearer access token) ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ Mobile (Flutter) │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────► │ │──► PostgreSQL (Prisma) └────────────────────┘ │ API (NestJS) │──► Cloudflare R2 (files) ┌────────────────────┐ HTTPS /admin/v1/* (cookie + TOTP 2FA) │ apps/api — the judge │──► SMS / e-mail providers │ Admin Web (Next.js)│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────► │ of every rule │──► Chargily / SATIM payments └────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────┘ PDFs and photos go straight between the apps and R2 with short-lived signed URLs the API hands out.

2.4 Inside apps/api

  • src/main.ts — starts the server. src/app.setup.ts — HTTP settings shared with the tests. src/app.module.ts — assembles everything.
  • src/config/ — reads and validates the environment variables (env.ts).
  • src/common/ — small shared helpers: the error envelope, client info, CSV and search text.
  • src/infrastructure/ — technical services every module may use: the database client, cryptography, background jobs, rate limits, e-mail and SMS, token verification.
  • src/modules/ — the 20 domain modules, one per business area. Each owns its tables and exposes only what its index.ts exports.
  • src/scripts/ — command-line tools: create an admin, generate the OpenAPI contract, seed demo data, Medicalcul extraction and import.
  • prisma/schema.prisma — every table, grouped by owning module.

The list of modules is one file:

2.6 Running everything on your machine

From the repository root, once:

npm install # installs API, Admin Web and packages cp apps/api/.env.example apps/api/.env # then fill DATABASE_URL and fresh 32+ char secrets cp apps/admin/.env.example apps/admin/.env npm run prisma:migrate:deploy -w @doktool/api # creates the tables npm run admin:create -w @doktool/api -- --email you@example.dz --name "Your Name"

Then, in three terminals:

npm run start:dev -w @doktool/api # API on http://localhost:3000 (Swagger at /docs) npm run dev -w @doktool/admin # Admin Web on http://localhost:3001 cd apps/mobile flutter pub get dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs flutter gen-l10n flutter run --dart-define=API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000
Sample data. npm run demo:seed -w @doktool/api fills a database whose name ends in _demo with demonstration accounts and content (it refuses any other database). The passwords it prints are shown once.

2.7 The one command that checks everything

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://…/doktool_test npm run ci cd apps/mobile && flutter analyze && flutter test

npm run ci runs, in order: Prettier formatting, ESLint, TypeScript type checks, the i18n parity check (every key in both languages), the design-token checks (no raw colour, radius, blur or duration in the code), the OpenAPI drift check, the admin client drift check, then every test of every workspace. At the end of the October 2026 audit it was green: 613 API tests, 30 Admin Web tests, the package tests, and 167 Flutter tests.

3. The architecture in one chapter

Before reading modules one by one, it helps to follow one request from the phone to the database and back, and to know the handful of mechanisms every feature reuses: tokens, the access decision, the error envelope, file storage, background jobs, messages and offline copies.

3.1 The life of one request

Take the doctor opening a prescription model on the phone. This is what happens, file by file:

PHONE API DATABASE / R2 reference_viewer_screen.dart └ openedReferenceProvider └ ReferenceFiles.download(id) └ generated client GET /v1/reference-documents/{id}/file-url └ AuthInterceptor adds "Authorization: Bearer <access token>" ─────────► ViewerAuthGuard: token valid? session live? ReferenceLibraryController.fileUrl() └ ReferenceDocumentsService.fileUrl() reads the published row ──► PostgreSQL └ AccessService.decideItems() policy evaluated again: AVAILABLE or LOCKED? └ StorageService.getSignedReadUrl() 10-minute signed URL ◄───────── { url, sha256, … } (or { error: { code: "FEATURE_LOCKED" … } }) └ dio GET signed url (no token) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────► R2 bucket └ SHA-256 of the bytes == published sha256 ? else refuse to show └ pdfrx draws the pages (no download, print or share button)

Three ideas are visible in this one example and repeat everywhere:

  1. The guard proves who is calling (a user token, a demo token or an admin cookie).
  2. The access policy decides what they may do, again, on this exact request.
  3. Files never pass through the API: it hands out a short signed URL, and the client checks the file's fingerprint.

3.2 Three kinds of identity

WhoProofLifetimeWhere in the code
A signed-in user (mobile)A JWT access token in Authorization: Bearer, plus a rotating refresh token kept in the phone's Keychain/KeystoreAccess 15 min; refresh rotates on every use and is bound to the device's installation idinfrastructure/security/user-tokens.ts, modules/auth/sessions.service.ts, mobile core/auth/
A demo visitor (mobile)A demo access token + a renewal tokenAccess 1 hour, renewed silentlyinfrastructure/security/demo-tokens.ts, modules/demo/
An admin (Admin Web)An HTTP-only session cookie obtained after password and a TOTP codeIdle and absolute limitsmodules/admin-auth/

The user guard is short enough to read whole. Notice that it only proves identity — it does not decide access:

And the token check also asks the database whether the session is still live, so a sign-out, a password change or a suspension takes effect on the very next request rather than when the 15-minute token expires:

Refresh tokens are single-use. Using one twice, or from another device, revokes the whole session — this is how a stolen refresh token is detected:

3.3 The access decision

Access is computed, never stored. AccessService.profileFor(viewer) gathers three facts — the account (status, professional type), the verification cases and the current subscription — and gives them to a pure function, evaluateAccess, together with the policy table. Chapter 6 reads that table line by line. What matters here: every content endpoint calls it, and the mobile app receives the result from GET /v1/me/access only to draw locks.

3.4 One error format for everything

Every refusal is a DomainError with a stable code (FEATURE_LOCKED, OTP_INVALID, SESSION_INVALID…). The global ErrorFilter turns any exception into the same JSON:

HTTP 403 { "error": { "code": "FEATURE_LOCKED", "message": "for developers only", "details": { "lockReason": "…" } } }

The apps never show message; they translate code with their own catalogue (mobile ApiError + commonErrorText, admin useErrorText).

3.5 Files: R2, signed URLs and upload intents

All files (reference PDFs, profile photos, verification documents, recovery photos) are in Cloudflare R2, reached only through StorageService. Two buckets exist: doktool-content (reference PDFs, photos) and doktool-private (identity documents). Nothing is public. Uploads follow the same three steps everywhere:

  1. The client declares the file (purpose, size, type, SHA-256). The API records an upload intent and answers with a signed PUT URL valid 15 minutes.
  2. The client sends the bytes straight to R2.
  3. The client confirms; the API checks size, type and the first bytes' signature (a PDF must start with %PDF), then attaches the file to its record.

3.6 Background jobs

Work that must happen later or regularly runs in pg-boss, a job queue stored in PostgreSQL itself (no Redis, ADR-007). Each module registers its own schedules when it starts:

JobScheduleWhat it does
reference-library sweepevery minuteProcesses uploaded PDFs: page count, checksum, file status.
auth.account-recoveryevery 10 minApplies approved recoveries once their 24-hour hold is over.
billing.reconcile-checkoutsevery 10 minAsks the gateway about payments still pending.
billing.advance-subscriptionsdaily 02:30Reminders, grace period, end of subscriptions.
verification.expire-and-reminddaily 06:17Expiry reminders and expirations of verifications.
verification.purge-documents, storage.purge-expired-uploads, auth.purge-expired, users.purge-unconfirmed, notifications.purge-old…hourly / dailyDelete what the retention rules say must not be kept.

3.7 Messages to people

Codes and security notices go out by e-mail (SMTP) or SMS (Infobip or Twilio, with a fallback, ADR-022) through MessageDelivery. Their texts come from server catalogue keys (server.security.…) in the account's language. In-app notifications are rows of the notifications table holding a catalogue key and parameters — never free text.

3.8 Offline

Every real account (students included) can keep, on the phone, the reference PDFs it may open, the published calculator versions and the pregnancy profiles it opened. The API publishes an offline manifest (GET /v1/offline/manifest): what this person may keep, with a version and a SHA-256 for each item. The app's OfflineSyncController downloads what is missing or changed, deletes the rest, and always shows the data version and whether what you see is live or cached.

3.9 How modules are allowed to depend on each other

Modular monolith (ADR-001). One server, but each module owns its tables. Another module may use it only through what its index.ts exports — usually a service with a few read methods. That is why, for example, AccessService asks UsersService.getAccessFacts() instead of reading the users table itself. A unit test checks that every Prisma model sits in the section of the module that owns it.
auth ──► users ◄── verification ◄── access ──► billing │ ▲ ▲ ▲ │ ▼ │ │ │ ▼ demo admin ───────────┘ │ finance │ reference-library, calculators, pregnancy, search, activity, offline ── all ask access for decisions storage, audit, notifications, analytics ── used by many, depend on nobody's tables

4. How the API is built — NestJS, using DokTool's own code

NestJS is a framework that organises a Node.js server into modules, each made of controllers (HTTP endpoints), services (the logic) and DTOs (the shapes of what comes in and goes out). Nest builds every object and hands it what it needs through its constructor — dependency injection. This chapter teaches those pieces with the smallest complete module of DokTool: notifications.

4.1 Start-up: main.ts and app.setup.ts

The server starts in main.ts. It reads the environment once, builds the application from AppModule, applies the shared HTTP settings and listens:

loadEnv (in config/env.ts) validates every environment variable with a Zod schema: a missing secret or a malformed URL stops the server at start-up instead of failing later. configureApp is shared with the integration tests, so tests run the exact same HTTP stack as production:

Read it line by line: helmet() adds security headers; cookieParser() reads the admin session cookie; payment webhooks keep their raw bytes (their signature is computed over them); the global ValidationPipe rejects any field a DTO does not declare (forbidNonWhitelisted) and converts types (transform); the global ErrorFilter gives every error the same shape; Swagger is served at /docs outside production.

4.2 The root module

The infrastructure modules come first (configuration, database, jobs, cryptography, rate limits, messaging, token security, health), then the 20 domain modules. Most infrastructure modules are global: their services can be injected anywhere without importing the module.

4.3 A module: notifications

A module declares its controllers, its providers (services) and what it exports to other modules. This one also schedules a daily clean-up job when it starts:

Other modules must import only from index.ts — the module's public door:

4.4 A controller: endpoints and guards

A controller maps URLs to methods. Decorators (the @… lines) tell Nest the HTTP verb, the guard to run first, and tell Swagger how to document the endpoint:

  • @Controller(`${USER_API_PREFIX}/me/notifications`) — every route here starts with /v1/me/notifications.
  • @UseGuards(UserAuthGuard) — a valid user token is required (a demo token is not enough: demos have no notifications).
  • @CurrentUser() user — injects the principal the guard stored on the request (userId, sessionId).
  • @Query() query: NotificationListQuery — the query string, validated against the DTO class.
  • @Param('id', new ParseUUIDPipe()) — the URL id, refused unless it is a UUID.
  • @HttpCode(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) — answers 204 with no body.
Controllers stay thin. In DokTool a controller only translates HTTP into a service call and the service's result into a DTO. Every rule lives in services, so it can be tested and reused.

4.5 DTOs: the contract

A DTO is a class with decorated fields. class-validator decorators (@IsOptional, @IsISO8601…) check incoming data; @ApiProperty describes the field in the OpenAPI contract, from which the mobile and admin clients are generated. Changing a DTO therefore changes both apps' generated code.

The static from() turns an internal record into exactly what the client may see (dates as ISO text, parameters as strings).

4.6 A service and the database

Services are @Injectable() classes. The constructor lists what they need; Nest provides it. Here the only dependency is PrismaService, the single database client:

Prisma turns the models of prisma/schema.prisma into a typed client: this.prisma.notification.findMany(…) is checked by the compiler against the table's columns. The model behind this service:

Note the conventions used in the whole schema: UUID v7 identifiers, snake_case column names mapped from camelCase fields, timestamps with time zone, and an index shaped exactly like the list query (user, unread, newest first).

4.7 Guards and decorators you will see everywhere

Decorator / guardWhereWhat it does
@UseGuards(UserAuthGuard) + @CurrentUser()user-only routesValid user token; the principal is { userId, sessionId }.
@UseGuards(ViewerAuthGuard) + @CurrentViewer()content routesA user token or a demo token; the viewer says which.
@RequireFeature('offline.sync')feature routesViewer guard + the access policy: refuses with FEATURE_LOCKED and the unlock path.
@RequireGrants('finance.read') + @CurrentAdmin()admin routesAdmin session cookie, origin check, and the listed grants.

4.8 Refusing: DomainError

Services never build HTTP responses. They throw new DomainError('CODE', 'developer message', details?); the code decides the HTTP status:

4.9 How the API is tested

  • Unit tests (apps/api/test/unit): pure logic without a database — the access policy matrix, the calculator engine, CSV cells, payment gateway parsing, search ranking.
  • Integration tests (apps/api/test/integration/*.e2e.spec.ts): the real application (configureApp included) against a real PostgreSQL test database, driven over HTTP with supertest. Helpers in actors.ts create a doctor, a student, an admin with given grants…, and content.ts publishes test content.
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://…/doktool_test" npx vitest run --project unit DATABASE_URL="postgresql://…/doktool_test" npx vitest run --project integration test/integration/activity.e2e.spec.ts

5. Accounts: sign-up, sign-in, sessions, recovery, deletion

Two modules hold accounts. users owns the account rows (names, contacts, professional profile, preferences). auth owns everything that proves who someone is: codes, passwords, sessions, refresh tokens, contact changes, recovery and deletion (ADR-009, ADR-023).

5.1 One field for e-mail or phone

People sign up with an e-mail or an Algerian mobile number, typed in the same field. Everything starts by normalising it:

E-mails are lower-cased; 0555 12 34 56 becomes +213555123456 (E.164). The channel (EMAIL or SMS) then decides how codes are sent.

5.2 Sign-up in two steps

App API DB / providers SignUpScreen « Créer mon compte » POST /v1/auth/sign-up {firstName, lastName, identifier, password, wilayaCode, termsVersion, language} AuthService.signUp parse identifier, password ≠ identifier, terms version current UsersService: create (or restart) an UNCONFIRMED account OtpService.issue(SIGN_UP) ─────────────► code by e-mail / SMS ◄─ { challengeId, destinationHint "a•••@x.dz", resendAvailableAt, expiresAt } OtpScreen (6 boxes) POST /v1/auth/sign-up/confirm {challengeId, code, deviceId} OtpService.consume → contact confirmed DemoService.markConverted(deviceId) (if this phone ran a demo) SessionsService.open → access + refresh tokens ◄─ AuthTokens RoleSelectScreen « Qui êtes-vous ? » → PUT professional profile → verification

An unconfirmed account that is never confirmed is deleted by the users.purge-unconfirmed job. Signing up again with the same identifier restarts it instead of failing — someone who lost the first code is not stuck.

5.3 One-time codes

OtpService serves four purposes: sign-up, password reset, contact change and account recovery. Its rules: 6 digits; the code itself is never stored (only an HMAC bound to the challenge); 60 seconds between sends and at most 5 sends; 3 wrong codes lock the challenge for 10 minutes; a challenge can only be consumed for its own purpose.

No account enumeration. « Mot de passe oublié » always answers with a challenge, even for an identifier with no account — in that case nothing is sent (delivers()), but the answer looks identical, so nobody can test which e-mails have an account.

5.4 Sign-in, lockout and sessions

Read it as a checklist: a rate limit per IP and per identifier; five wrong passwords lock the account for 15 minutes (ACCOUNT_LOCKED with retryAt); suspended and unconfirmed accounts are refused with their own codes; a success opens a session bound to the device's installation id and — important for recovery — cancels any account recovery someone else started.

A session is a row of user_sessions with its refresh tokens in refresh_tokens (only their SHA-256). The API can list a person's sessions (GET /v1/me/sessions) and end one (DELETE /v1/me/sessions/:sessionId); the V1 app does not show this list yet, but a password change, a recovery or a suspension use the same revocation. Because UserTokens.verify checks the session on every request, the other device is out at its very next call.

5.5 Changing contacts and password

AccountSecurityService (Settings › « Sécurité du compte ») follows one principle: every change asks for the current password, so a borrowed unlocked phone cannot take over the account; and every change is announced on the other contact, so the owner learns about it even if the attacker controls one channel.

5.6 Assisted recovery: « J'ai perdu l'accès aux deux »

When someone has lost both their e-mail and their phone, a human checks their identity:

1 start lost contact + first/last name + NEW contact → code sent to the new contact 2 confirm code proves the new contact → recovery token (60 min to finish) 3 photos identity document + selfie → private bucket (JPEG/PNG, 10 MB, signed upload) 4 submit request goes to Admin Web « Récupération » answer promised within 72 h 5 review admin compares photos with the verified identity → approve (note) or reject (reason) 6 hold 24 h the owner is told; signing in with the password CANCELS the request 7 apply job every 10 min: new contact replaces the old ones, password unusable, all devices out

The apply step is where the October 2026 audit found a race: the request is now claimed first (APPROVED → APPLIED in one conditional update), and only then are the contacts replaced. If the owner cancels at the same instant, the claim fails and nothing changes.

5.7 Deleting an account

Each module that holds personal data exposes an eraseUser(userId) method; deletion calls them all, anonymises the account row (finance and the audit log must keep their history, without a name), revokes every session and writes one audit entry. On the phone, the app then forgets every personal setting it kept (chapter 11).

5.8 The numbers, in one place

6. Access: who may open what

This is the most important chapter for understanding DokTool's behaviour. One table decides what each kind of person can open; one pure function applies it; every endpoint re-checks it; the apps only draw the answer. If you understand modules/access, you understand why a screen shows a lock, an explanation or a « Voir les offres » button.

6.1 The inputs

For a demo session, the only input is "this is a demo" (and which profession it previews). For a real account, AccessService gathers three facts in parallel, each from the module that owns it:

FactAsked fromContains
Account factsUsersService.getAccessFactsstatus (ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, DELETED), professional type (DOCTOR, RESIDENT, STUDENT or not chosen yet)
Verification snapshotVerificationStatusService.accessSnapshotfor IDENTITY, STUDENT_STATUS and PROFESSIONAL_STATUS: status, submission date, expiry, renewalPending
SubscriptionSubscriptionStatusService.currentstatus (ACTIVE, CANCELED, GRACE…), period end, grace end

6.2 The policy table

The whole V1 policy is data. Read it as a grid: one block per tier; in each, which content items open (content) and the state of each feature (features):

The content rules use three scopes: ALL (everything opens), STUDENT_TIER (items marked for students, plus samples), DEMO_SAMPLE (only items flagged demoSample), and NONE for a restricted account. A locked item always carries its lockReason and, when one exists, its unlockPath — the single screen that can help (sign up, see plans, start verification…). Students get explanations without an unlock path: no upsell (Lock L38).

6.3 Placing a person in one tier

placeInTier reads like the specification. Follow it from top to bottom with an example in mind — a verified doctor whose subscription ended last week:

  1. Not a demo. Account ACTIVE. Professional type chosen (DOCTOR). Identity not rejected.
  2. Not a student, so look at PROFESSIONAL_STATUS: VERIFIED.
  3. isSubscriptionLive: ACTIVE subscriptions stay live 7 days past their end while billing moves them to GRACE; GRACE stays live until its end. Last week → still live → PROFESSIONAL.
  4. After grace: not live. Verified, so purchase = 'OPEN' → PROFESSIONAL_UNPAID with « Renouveler » available.

6.4 Re-verification never interrupts access

A verification expires (professional status after a set period; see chapter 8). Renewing it opens a new case of the same type. Before the October 2026 audit, the newest case — still undecided — replaced the verified one, and a paying doctor fell to PROFESSIONAL_UNPAID the moment they tapped « Renouveler ». accessSnapshot now keeps the earlier decision counting while the new case is undecided, and flags renewalPending so purchase shows « vérification en cours »:

6.5 From tier to profile, and from profile to items

The result, AccessProfile, is what GET /v1/me/access returns to the app. Lists and detail endpoints then decide each item with decideItem:

Pure and tested as a matrix. access-policy.ts does no input/output at all: same inputs and time, same answer. test/unit/access-policy.matrix.spec.ts checks every tier against every feature and content rule. To change the policy: edit the table, bump version, update the matrix test.

6.6 Re-checking on every endpoint

Two mechanisms enforce the profile on the server:

  • @RequireFeature('…') on a route (chapter 4.7) refuses a locked feature before the handler runs.
  • Content services call AccessService.decideItems(viewer, items) and only return a PDF URL, a calculator definition or a profile's content when the item is AVAILABLE; a locked item is still listed, with its lock.

6.7 Viewers: user or demo

Read routes accept both kinds of token; write routes (favorites, history, verification, payments) use UserAuthGuard, which refuses demo tokens. Demo and user tokens are signed with the same key but have different audiences, so one can never pass for the other.

6.8 The demo

One device keeps one active demo session, identified by the phone's installation id. Nothing a demo does is written to user tables: its favorites live in the phone's memory only. When the same phone confirms a new account, markConverted closes the demo as CONVERTED, so the « Démo » analytics funnel can count conversions (another audit fix).

6.9 What the apps do with the profile

  • Mobile: AccessController loads the profile at launch, on resume and after verification or payment. Rows draw a LockLabel; tapping a locked row opens showLockSheet with the explanation and, if there is one, the single unlock action. Locks are never red.
  • Admin Web: the user drawer's « Accès » tab shows an account's profile and the inputs it came from (AccessService.explainForUser), so support can answer "why can't I open this?".

7. Content: reference PDFs, calculators, pregnancy, search, offline

The four resources of DokTool live in four modules — reference-library, calculators, pregnancy and (for finding them) search — helped by storage, clinical-review, activity and offline. Each has an app side (read-only, access-checked) and an admin side (authoring, review, publication, audited).

7.1 Reference library: ordonnances and certificates

A reference model is a PDF uploaded by the Super Admin, with minimal metadata: a French title (pre-filled from the file name), an optional English title, the demoSample flag and a status. The PDF is the content; nobody edits it in DokTool.

Admin Web « Ajouter un modèle » API R2 / DB 1 compute SHA-256 of the PDF in the browser 2 POST …/reference-documents/uploads ──► requestUpload: new id, upload intent, signed PUT (15 min) 3 PUT bytes ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────► doktool-content 4 POST …/reference-documents ──────────► create: confirm intent (size, %PDF-), create model + file v1 5 job "process file": download, SHA-256 = declared?, count pages → file READY, becomes the model's current file 6 « Activer » ─────────────────────────► changeStatus ENABLED (needs a processed PDF) → visible in the app

« Remplacer le PDF » creates the next file version under the same model id, so favorites, history and links keep working; earlier versions stay stored (immutable keys) and can still be previewed by admins.

7.2 StorageService: one door to files

No module imports the R2 SDK. They all use the abstract StorageService; R2StorageAdapter implements it in production and LocalStorageAdapter (files on disk, signed URLs served by the API itself) in development and tests:

7.3 Calculators: a formula as data

A calculator is never code. It is a definition — JSON validated by a Zod schema — that both engines (TypeScript on the server, Dart on the phone) interpret the same way. A definition holds:

  • inputs: NUMBER/INTEGER (with units from a sourced registry and three ranges: hard — impossible values; validated — where the formula was validated; plausible — beyond it, a « vérifiez la valeur » note), CHOICE (answers, optionally with points) and BOOLEAN;
  • cross-field rules (e.g. diastolic must be below systolic);
  • the formula, a tree over a closed set of operators;
  • the result (unit, decimals), the interpretation bands and the limitations.

There is no eval, no free-form expression and no operator outside these lists: a definition cannot do anything the engine does not know. checkDefinition then checks what a schema cannot: unique keys, known units, nested ranges, a well-typed formula, ordered bands that do not overlap.

The engine

Read the order: presence and types → hard ranges → cross-field rules → validated ranges → plausibility notes → formula → band. The engine never returns a result for invalid input or input outside the validated range: it returns the issues instead, and the app explains them. Rounding is "half away from zero" computed on the decimal text, so 2.675 rounds the same way in TypeScript and Dart.

Two engines, one truth. The TypeScript engine is authoritative: admins' test runs and publication use it. The Dart engine lets the phone compute offline; before using a version, the app runs the version's published test cases on its own engine (« self-test ») and refuses the calculator if one fails. packages/calculator-vectors holds shared cases both engines must pass in CI.

Governance: draft → review → published

DRAFT ──submit──► IN_REVIEW ──approve──► PUBLISHED ──retire──► RETIRED ▲ (author) │ (reviewer ≠ author) immutable: a change is a new version └──── return ────────┘ gate to submit: primary source + a passing test run of THIS definition (checksum) gate to publish: tests re-run on the server, sources, four-eyes, and 1 or 2 sign-offs (ADR-024)

A test run is stored with the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the definition it ran on (canonical-json.ts). Editing the definition changes the checksum, so an old green run no longer counts — it is impossible to submit a definition that was not tested as it is.

Double sign-off (clinical-review)

7.4 Grossesse · Allaitement

A substance (names, ATC code, synonyms, demoSample, enabled) has profile versions, governed like calculators (draft → review → published, author ≠ reviewer, optional second sign-off). A profile's content has two blocks: pregnancy (T1, T2, T3, peripartum) and lactation. For each period: a conduct (CONTRAINDICATED, AVOID, OCCASIONAL_USE or none) and, separately, an evidence level from 0 (« Absence de données ») to 4 (« Données robustes ») with its sources — never merged into a "safe" verdict.

Three more tools exist on the admin side:

  • Spreadsheet import (ADR-025): an uploaded XLSX becomes a preview batch; the admin maps columns and status words, corrects rows, then commits — which writes drafts, never published content.
  • Merging duplicates (ADR-027): a duplicate substance's names become synonyms of the one kept; favorites and links of the duplicate open the kept substance; the merge can be undone.
  • User reports (« Signaler une erreur » in the app) arrive in a queue the clinical team resolves.

7.5 Search

Global search (GET /v1/search?q=…) runs over enabled reference models, published calculators and listed substances, with the viewer's access on each hit (locked results stay in place). Ranking is in ranking.ts: text is normalised (lower case, no accents), each query word may have typos (none up to 2 letters, 1 up to 5, 2 above, Damerau-Levenshtein), exact and prefix matches score higher, and a query naming a category (« certificat… ») puts that group first. Nothing is ever boosted commercially.

7.6 Favorites and history

The phone records history entries locally and sends them in batches. A restricted (read-only) account's entries are dropped silently on purpose — the phone's queue must never get stuck on a refusal.

7.7 The offline manifest

The manifest's dataVersion is a fingerprint of everything in it: the phone compares it with the version it stored to know whether anything changed, and shows it in « Données et hors ligne ».

8. Verification, payments, finance, analytics, audit, admin security

These modules turn a sign-up into a paying professional and give the team the tools to run the service: checking diplomas, taking payments, counting money, measuring use without spying, keeping an unchangeable log of every admin action, and protecting the console itself.

8.1 Verification

A person proves two things, in separate cases: their identity (national ID, passport, or student card for students) and their status — enrolment for a student (STUDENT_STATUS), residency or the Ordre des médecins for a resident or doctor (PROFESSIONAL_STATUS).

PREPARING ──submit──► SUBMITTED ──claim──► IN_REVIEW ──approve──► VERIFIED ──(expiry)──► EXPIRED ▲ │ renew: a new case from 60 days before └──────── start again ◄──── reject (reason)┘ after 2 rejections: APPEALED → decided by a DIFFERENT reviewer

On the reviewer's side (VerificationReviewService), a reviewer claims a case (so two people never decide the same one), views documents in a restricted viewer (60-second signed URLs, a watermark with the reviewer's name, every view audited), then approves or rejects with a reason code. Approval copies the proven role and details to the profile and schedules the documents' deletion: files are kept only as long as the retention rule says.

8.2 Billing: plans, checkout, gateways

Plans are versioned: the Super Admin publishes a plan version with its price, duration and « inclus / non inclus » lines; a price change is a new version, and running subscriptions keep theirs. Checkout is open only to an active, professionally verified doctor or resident (students never pay; nobody pays before verification — ADR-006 Q6).

App « Payer » (plan, CIB or Edahabia, acknowledgement « non remboursable ») POST /v1/subscription/checkout ─► CheckoutService.start eligibility, plan on sale, method available transaction DT-2026-000123 (PENDING) gateway.register(order) ─────────────► Chargily / SATIM ◄─ { redirectUrl } ─────────────────────────────────────── payment page browser: the person pays ON THE GATEWAY'S PAGE (the API never sees card data) return URL / webhook / reconcile job (every 10 min) ─► settle(transaction) gateway.status(reference) ← the only truth PAID → activate: subscription starts or extends PaymentResultScreen polls GET /v1/subscription/transactions/:transactionId until final

Each gateway (ChargilyGateway, SatimGateway, and FakeGateway outside production) implements this class. A webhook is accepted only with a valid signature computed over the raw body, and even then the API asks the gateway for the order's status instead of trusting the notification.

No refund anywhere. There is no refund status, endpoint or button. A real exception (law, accounting, provider error) is an exceptional adjustment in Finance, requested by the Super Admin and counted only once a second admin approves it.

8.3 Finance

Finance reads transactions (it never changes them) and adds what the business needs around them: payment fees (estimated from a rate per gateway × card, later replaced by the provider's statement), operating expenses (voided, never deleted), exceptional adjustments (two admins) and CSV reports. The ledger always has the same shape (Lock L40):

CSV cells go through csvCell(), which neutralises text a spreadsheet would run as a formula (= + - @) — an audit fix.

8.4 Analytics without spying

The app sends only event names with counts, codes and flags. The server adds the envelope from its own facts: a keyed hash of the person (stable, not reversible), tier, profession, specialty, wilaya. Each event type has a strict schema; anything else is dropped. Dashboards hide any cell behind fewer than 10 people (« < 10 »).

8.5 The audit log

Every admin change calls audit.record({...}) with who, what, which record, before/after and the reason the admin typed. The database table itself refuses UPDATE and DELETE, so even a bug cannot rewrite history.

8.6 Admin security: password, TOTP, grants

/sign-in email + password ─► AdminAuthService.signIn lockout after 5 failures; same timing for unknown e-mails ◄─ 5-minute challenge: ENROL (first time: QR code) or VERIFY 6-digit TOTP code ───► completeTotp ─► opaque session cookie (idle + absolute timeouts) every admin request: AdminBoundaryGuard (no bearer tokens; writes only from the Admin Web origin) AdminSessionGuard (live session + the route's @RequireGrants)

Grants are given per admin, from presets (Super Admin, Verification reviewer, Library manager, Calculator editor, Clinical reviewer…) adjustable one by one; a grant can also be temporary (a few hours). Separation of duties is checked both in Admin Web (live, before saving) and by the API.

8.7 The admin module

modules/admin holds read-only screens that combine several modules: « Vue d'ensemble » (the ledger strip and work lists), « Utilisateurs » (search and the user drawer: profile, access with its inputs, subscriptions, activity counts), and the audit log with its CSV export.

9. How Admin Web is built — Next.js, React and the console kit

Admin Web is a Next.js application written in React and TypeScript. It has no database and no business rule of its own: every screen reads and writes through the API, and every button it hides is also refused by the API. Its job is to make the team's work fast, clear and safe.

9.1 The layers

src/app/ URLs. A folder = a route; page.tsx = the page. Thin: grant check + feature component. admin/layout.tsx every console page inside ConsoleShell (top bar + navigation) admin/users/page.tsx /admin/users → <RequireGrant grant="users.read"><UsersPage/> sign-in/ the two-step sign-in (password, then authenticator code) src/features/<section>/ the screens: pages, drawers, dialogs, labels, small helpers src/ui/ the console kit: Button, Badge, DataTable, Dialog, Drawer, Field, Tabs, Toast… src/api/client.ts typed calls: api.GET('/admin/v1/users', …) checked against schema.d.ts src/session/session.ts who is signed in (useMe) and what they may do (useGrants) src/i18n/ FR/EN messages from packages/i18n, formatting of dates, money, bytes src/shell/ ConsoleShell, the navigation list, RequireGrant src/proxy.ts no session cookie → straight to /sign-in

9.2 One origin: the API behind Admin Web

The browser never calls the API's domain. Next.js forwards /admin/v1/* to the API, so the session cookie (__Host-doktool_admin, HTTP-only) belongs to Admin Web's own origin and every write carries Admin Web's Origin header — which the API's boundary guard checks. A strict Content-Security-Policy allows scripts only from the console itself.

9.3 Calling the API

openapi-fetch is typed by schema.d.ts, generated from the API contract: a wrong path, a missing parameter or a misspelled field is a compile error. call() turns any failure into an ApiFailure carrying the API's error code:

Errors are shown with useErrorText() (src/ui/errors.ts), which maps codes to catalogue sentences — never the server's developer message. If a call answers "session ended", the provider reloads the sign-in page and remembers where the admin was.

9.4 Server state with TanStack Query

Every list and detail is a useQuery (or useInfiniteQuery for paged lists) with a query key. Every change is a useMutation; on success it invalidates or updates the keys it affects, so every screen showing that data refreshes. Read the users page's list as the model for all lists:

useDebounced waits 300 ms after the last key before asking the server (an audit fix: it used to ask at every key).

9.5 Who sees what: grants in the UI

  • The navigation (shell/nav.ts) lists each section with the grant it needs; sections the admin lacks are not shown.
  • A page wraps its content in <RequireGrant>: typing the URL without the grant shows a clear message instead of failing API calls.
  • Buttons check has('…'). This is only comfort: the API refuses anyway.

9.6 The console kit (src/ui)

ComponentRole
ButtonVariants primary · secondary · ghost · danger · teal; busy shows a spinner and blocks double clicks.
DataTableSortable table with keyboard navigation; a row can open a drawer. Clicks on controls inside a row no longer also open the row (audit fix A2).
Drawer / DialogSide panel for a record's detail; centred dialog for a decision. Both trap focus and close with Escape.
ReasonDialogEvery admin change asks for a reason (3–500 characters) that goes into the audit log.
Field, TextInput, Select, SwitchLabelled, accessible form controls; errors under the field with an icon.
Badge, Alert, EmptyState, Skeleton, PageHeaderStatus words with colour (never colour alone), messages, empty and loading states.
PeriodPicker, charts, MetricTileFinance and analytics periods, bar/line charts with a table fallback, ledger figures.
PdfPagesDraws a PDF on canvases from a signed URL — preview without download or print.

9.7 Forms

Forms use React Hook Form with a Zod schema holding the same limits as the API (lengths, patterns). The API stays the judge: its VALIDATION_FAILED field errors are put back under the matching fields with fieldErrors().

9.8 Signing in

app/sign-in/sign-in-form.tsx has two steps. The password step answers with a challenge: ENROL the first time (a QR code drawn from the otpauth:// link, to scan with an authenticator app) or VERIFY afterwards. The six-digit code then creates the session cookie. If the 5-minute challenge expires or locks, the form now says why before starting again (audit fix A5).

9.9 Languages and formatting

Messages come from the same catalogue as the app (packages/i18n), under admin.* keys: t('admin.users.title'). A key that does not exist is a compile error (MessageKey type). src/i18n/format.ts formats dates, numbers, money (DZD), file sizes and ages in the chosen language.

10. Admin Web, screen by screen

Each section of the console has a folder in apps/admin/src/features/, a route in src/app/admin/, a grant that opens it and an API controller behind it. For each screen: what it is for, every button, and which API call it makes. Appendix A lists every one of these buttons again with its line number.
